lessons.title: Preventing and controlling animal diseases
lessons.html:
Disease prevention and control

This Diploma in Animal Health (NQF 6) prepares animal health technicians who prevent and control animal diseases and support veterinarians in the field. The work protects farm income, food security, export markets and public health.

How diseases spread

  • Direct contact between animals, e.g. at shared grazing, water points or auctions.
  • Vectors such as ticks (heartwater, redwater, gallsickness) and biting insects (lumpy skin disease, bluetongue, African horse sickness).
  • Contaminated objects: vehicles, boots, equipment, feed and water.
  • Movement of animals from infected areas, which is why movement controls are central to disease control.
  • Wildlife: buffalo can carry foot-and-mouth disease and bovine TB, and warthogs and ticks are linked to African swine fever.

The control toolbox

ToolExample
VaccinationAnthrax and blackleg in cattle, brucellosis in heifers
Vector controlDipping, pour-ons, fly control
BiosecurityQuarantine new animals, footbaths, restricted access
Movement controlPermits, quarantine areas, disease control zones
Testing and cullingBovine TB and brucellosis testing of herds
SurveillanceRoutine inspections, sampling at dip tanks and abattoirs

The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 gives the state the powers to declare controlled diseases, set control measures and restrict movement. Technicians apply these measures in the field under the direction of the state veterinarian.

lessons.title: Supporting the veterinarian in the field
lessons.html:
Field support

Animal health technicians are often the vet's eyes and hands in rural districts. Typical tasks include herd inspections, collecting blood and tissue samples, tuberculin testing under supervision, vaccination campaigns, movement permit checks and outbreak response.

Responding to a suspected outbreak

  1. Recognise: e.g. several cattle salivating and lame with blisters on the mouth and feet may indicate foot-and-mouth disease.
  2. Report immediately to the state veterinarian.
  3. Stop movement of animals, products and vehicles from the farm.
  4. Protect yourself and avoid becoming a carrier: protective clothing, disinfecting boots and vehicle, not visiting other farms the same day.
  5. Collect information: number of animals sick and dead, when signs started, recent purchases or movements.
  6. Support control measures as instructed: sampling, quarantine, vaccination or culling.

Taking good samples

A laboratory result is only as good as the sample. Label every tube with animal ID, farm, date and sample type. Use the right container, keep samples cool as instructed and send them quickly with a completed submission form. A badly labelled sample wastes time during an outbreak.

Records and reporting

Record every vaccination, test and inspection: farm, number and ID of animals, product and batch number. These records prove that a region is controlling disease, which matters for export certification of beef, wool, game and ostrich products.

Safety

Work in crushes and handling facilities is risky. Never put your arm between the bars of a crush while an animal is moving, work in pairs, and use protective gear when handling possible zoonoses such as anthrax, brucellosis and rabies.

Key points

  • Diseases spread by contact, vectors, objects, animal movement and wildlife.
  • Control tools include vaccination, vector control, biosecurity, movement control, testing and surveillance.
  • Report suspected controlled diseases immediately and stop movement.
  • Well-labelled samples and complete records support control and exports.
  • Protect yourself in the crush and from zoonoses.
